🧩 Unit 1 · Grammar: Present and past tenses

🎯 Goal

You will learn to talk about your routines, what is happening now, and your experiences.

📘 1. Present simple and present continuous

TenseUse it forExample
Present simple
I work / she works		habits, routines, factsI study English every evening.
Present continuous
am / is / are + -ing		actions happening now, or around nowI am studying English right now.

💡 Time words

always, usually, often, every day, never (present simple) · now, at the moment, today, this week (present continuous).

⚠️ Watch out!

Some verbs do not usually go in the continuous form. They are state verbs: know, like, love, want, need, understand, believe. Say I know the answer, not I am knowing.

📘 2. Past simple and present perfect

TenseUse it forExample
Past simple
worked / went		a finished action at a clear time in the pastI visited London in 2022.
Present perfect
have / has + past participle		experience, or a past action that matters now. The time is not important.I have visited London twice.

for or since? Use for + a time period (for three years). Use since + a starting point (since 2020).

Irregular verbs to remember: be – was/were – been · do – did – done · go – went – gone · see – saw – seen · eat – ate – eaten · write – wrote – written · take – took – taken

💡 Time words

yesterday, last week, in 2022, two days ago (past simple) · ever, never, already, yet, just, so far, since, for (present perfect).

⚠️ Common mistake

I have seen him yesterday. ✗ → I saw him yesterday. ✓ When you say exactly when, use the past simple.

📄 A new hobby

Last year, Marta, a 28-year-old office worker from Cēsis, felt tired and stressed. She worked long hours and spent most evenings on the sofa looking at her phone. "I had no energy and no hobbies," she says.

Then a colleague invited her to a Saturday morning running group. Marta did not want to go at first, but she went and met a friendly group of people. They run five kilometres, and afterwards they have coffee together. "I couldn't run for five minutes at the start," Marta says. "Now I can run for forty minutes without stopping."

Marta has changed her routine. She now goes to bed earlier, and she doesn't stay up late on her phone. She has also made three new friends. This year she has already run in two city races, and she is training for a half marathon in October. "Running is not only about being fit," she says. "It makes me feel happy. 📝 Unit 1 · Writing: informal and formal emails

🎯 Goal

You will learn to write informal and formal emails about free time and routines, using present and past tenses and linking words.

📘 1. Formal or informal?

We choose our words for the reader. We write informal emails to friends and family. We write formal emails to a boss, a teacher, a company or someone we do not know.

Informal (friends)Formal (work, school, companies)
Hi Anna, / Dear Anna,Dear Mr Brown, / Dear Ms Smith, / Dear Sir or Madam,
Thanks for your email. / Great to hear from you!Thank you for your email. / I am writing to ask about ...
Can you ...? / Could you ...?Could you please ...? / I would be grateful if you could ...
I'm sorry, but I can't ...Unfortunately, I am unable to ...
Write soon! / See you! / Take care,I look forward to hearing from you. / Thank you for your help.
Love, / Best wishes, / Bye for now,Yours sincerely, (name known) / Yours faithfully, (name not known)

Tips: In informal emails you can use short forms (I'm, can't), phrasal verbs and exclamation marks. In formal emails use full forms (I am, cannot), polite words (please, would, could) and no slang.

📘 2. A good email has four parts

  1. Greeting – Dear ... / Hi ...
  2. Reason – why you are writing (1 sentence)
  3. Main part – the details, one idea in each paragraph
  4. Ending – a closing sentence and a sign-off

📘 3. Coherence and cohesion

Coherence means your ideas are in a clear order and the reader can follow them. Use paragraphs. Put one idea in each paragraph.

Cohesion means the sentences are joined with small words. Use linking words:

UseLinking words
addingand, also, too, as well as, in addition, moreover (formal)
contrastbut, however, although, on the other hand, in spite of
reason / resultbecause, so, as, therefore, that is why
orderfirst, then, after that, finally, at the end
examplefor example, for instance, such as

Also use reference words so you do not repeat nouns: My brother has a new job. He likes it very much. This is good news.

📘 4. Unit 1 examples

✉️ Informal email

Task: Your friend Sam asked what you do in your free time. Write back and invite him to join you.

Hi Sam,

Thanks for your email – great to hear from you! You asked about my free time. Well, I usually go to the gym after work, and at the weekend I hang out with friends. I have also taken up cycling, and I love it!

Last Saturday we cycled thirty kilometres to the lake. It was tiring, but we had a lovely picnic. Why don't you join us next weekend? Let me know if you can come.

Write soon!
Anna

✉️ Formal email

Task: You want to join a sports club. Write to the club manager and ask about the classes and the price.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to ask about the classes at your sports club. I live nearby, and I am looking for a new hobby. I have never done yoga before, so I would like to start with a class for beginners.

Could you please tell me when the classes are and how much they cost? In addition, I would be grateful if you could send me information about membership.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Anna Ozola

💡 Notice

The informal email uses short forms (don't), exclamation marks and Write soon!. The formal email uses I am writing to ..., Could you please ...? and Yours faithfully. Both use present simple (routines), present perfect (experience) and past simple (last Saturday).

✏️ Practice

[h5p slug="b1-unit-1-writing-choose-the-right-register"]

Task 2: Mark the linking words

[h5p slug="b1-unit-1-writing-find-the-linking-words"]

Task 3: Complete the email with linking words

[h5p slug="b1-unit-1-writing-complete-the-email"]

✍️ Your turn

Choose one email (100–120 words) and hand it in in the Writing assignment that follows this lesson.

✉️ Option A: informal

Write to a friend. Tell them about your routine, a new hobby you have started, and what you did last weekend. Invite them to do something together.

✉️ Option B: formal

Write to a language school. Ask about evening English classes. Say who you are, what you do in the week, and ask about the price and the start date.

Checklist: ☐ greeting ☐ reason for writing ☐ paragraphs ☐ 3 linking words ☐ correct register ☐ unit grammar ☐ unit vocabulary ☐ sign-off

🧩 Unit 2 · Grammar: Past continuous, past perfect and story linkers

🎯 Goal

You will learn to tell a story about the past and say what happened first, what was happening, and what happened next.

📘 1. Past continuous

Form: was / were + verb-ing. I was walking. They were waiting.

Use it for an action that was in progress at a moment in the past, or a background action: At 8 o'clock, I was packing my bag.

Use it with the past simple when a short action interrupts a long action: I was walking to the station when I saw my teacher.

📘 2. Past perfect

Form: had + past participle. I had left. She had never flown.

Use it for an action that happened before another action in the past: When we arrived at the airport, the plane had already left.

TensePictureExample
Past perfectfirst (earlier)We had booked the hotel...
Past simplesecond (later)...but when we arrived, it was closed.

📘 3. Linking words for stories

WordMeaningExample
whileat the same time as (a long action)While I was sleeping, the train stopped.
whenat the time; or afterWhen it started to rain, we went inside.
as soon asimmediately afterAs soon as we landed, I called my mum.
before / afterearlier / laterAfter we had eaten, we went for a walk.
by the timeat that moment, or beforeBy the time we got there, it had closed.
suddenly, finally, in the endstory wordsSuddenly, I heard a loud noise.

💡 Tip

Do not use the continuous with state verbs (I was knowing ✗). Use I knew ✓.

Last summer, Jānis and his girlfriend Kristīne booked a cheap package holiday to Greece. They had never been to Greece before, and they were very excited. At the airport, however, they heard bad news: their flight had a four-hour delay.

One day, while they were walking in the old town, they got lost. A friendly local woman showed them the way and even invited them for coffee.

  1. Greeting – Dear ... / Hi ...
  2. Reason – why you are writing (1 sentence)
  3. Main part – the details, one idea in each paragraph
  4. Ending – a closing sentence and a sign-off

📘 3. Coherence and cohesion

📘 4. Unit 2 examples

✉️ Informal email

Task: You have just come back from a holiday. Write to a friend and tell them about it.

Hi Laura,

How are you? I'm back from Greece – what a trip! First, our flight was late, so we arrived at the hotel after midnight. However, the next morning the sun was shining and we had breakfast with a lovely sea view.

While we were walking in the old town, we got lost, but a kind woman helped us. After that we had the best coffee ever! You should go there next summer.

Write soon and tell me your news!
Love,
Jānis

✉️ Formal email

Task: You had problems at a hotel last week. Write to the manager to complain and ask for your money back.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about my stay at your hotel from 3 to 7 July. When we arrived, our room had been given to another guest, and we had to take a room next to a noisy bar. As a result, we could not sleep.

Moreover, the air conditioning was not working during the whole stay. I would be grateful if you could refund part of the price.

I look forward to your reply.

Yours faithfully,

🧩 Unit 3 · Grammar: Talking about the future: will, going to, present continuous

🎯 Goal

You will learn to talk about plans, arrangements, predictions and quick decisions.

📘 1. Three ways to talk about the future

FormUse it forExample
will + verbquick decisions, offers, promises, predictions (opinions)It's cold. I'll close the window.
I think robots will do many jobs.
be going to + verbplans and intentions; predictions with evidenceI'm going to buy a new phone.
Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.
present continuous (am/is/are + -ing)fixed arrangements (time and place are decided)I'm meeting Anna at 6 p.m. tomorrow.

📘 2. How to choose

  • Did you decide before speaking? Use going to. I'm going to learn Spanish.
  • Do you decide now, while speaking? Use will. Oh no, I forgot milk! I'll go to the shop.
  • Is it in your calendar, with a time or place? Use the present continuous. We're flying to Oslo on Friday.

📘 3. Negatives and questions

will: I won't (will not) forget. Will you help me?
going to: She isn't going to come. Are you going to study tonight?

📘 4. Useful future words

Words for predictions: probably, definitely, maybe, perhaps, I think, I expect, I'm sure. Put probably after will: It will probably rain. But before won't: It probably won't rain.

💡 Time words

tomorrow, next week, in two years, soon, by 2030, in the future.

⚠️ Common mistake

After when, as soon as, before, if we do not use will. Say When I arrive, I'll call you (not When I will arrive).

🎯 Goal

You will learn to write informal and formal emails about plans and technology, using future forms and linking words.

📘 1. Formal or informal?

We choose our words for the reader. We write informal emails to friends and family. We write formal emails to a boss, a teacher, a company or someone we do not know.

Tips: In informal emails you can use short forms (I'm, can't), phrasal verbs and exclamation marks. In formal emails use full forms (I am, cannot), polite words (please, would, could) and no slang.

📘 2. A good email has four parts

  1. Greeting – Dear ... / Hi ...
  2. Reason – why you are writing (1 sentence)
  3. Main part – the details, one idea in each paragraph
  4. Ending – a closing sentence and a sign-off

📘 3. Coherence and cohesion

Coherence means your ideas are in a clear order and the reader can follow them. Use paragraphs. Put one idea in each paragraph.

Cohesion means the sentences are joined with small words. Use linking words:

UseLinking words
addingand, also, too, as well as, in addition, moreover (formal)
contrastbut, however, although, on the other hand, in spite of
reason / resultbecause, so, as, therefore, that is why
orderfirst, then, after that, finally, at the end
examplefor example, for instance, such as

Also use reference words so you do not repeat nouns: My brother has a new job. He likes it very much. This is good news.

📘 4. Unit 3 examples

✉️ Informal email

Task: Your friend asked for help to choose a new phone. Write back with your advice and tell them your own plans.

Hi Marcis,

Thanks for your message! I'd buy the cheaper phone. Firstly, it has a good camera. Secondly, the battery lasts two days, so you won't need to charge it every night. Although the other phone has a bigger screen, it is much more expensive.

By the way, I'm going to get a new laptop next month, so I'll sell my old one cheaply if you want it. Let's talk about it on Friday – we're meeting at six, right?

Bye for now!
Ints

✉️ Formal email

Task: You saw an advertisement for a computer course. Write to the school to ask for information.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to ask about your computer course for adults, which I saw on your website. I am going to start a new job in September, and I will need to use spreadsheets and email every day.

Could you please tell me when the next course starts and how long it lasts? Furthermore, I would like to know whether the course is online or in the classroom.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Inese Ruka

💡 Notice

Both emails use future forms: I'm going to get (plan), I'll sell (offer), we're meeting (arrangement), I will need (prediction). Notice the linking words: firstly, secondly, although, by the way, furthermore.

🧩 Unit 4 · Grammar: Modal verbs: must, have to, should, might, can't

🎯 Goal

You will learn to talk about rules, advice, obligation, possibility and certainty.

📘 1. Modal verbs are special

After a modal verb we use the base verb (no to, no -s): She must wear a uniform. (not She must wears)

MeaningVerbExample
strong obligation (rules)must / have toYou must show your ID. Students have to be on time.
no obligationdon't have toYou don't have to wear a tie. (It is not necessary.)
it is forbiddenmustn'tYou mustn't use your phone in the exam.
adviceshould / shouldn'tYou should sleep more. You shouldn't work so late.
permission and abilitycan / could / mayCan I leave early? Could you help me?

⚠️ Be careful

mustn't and don't have to are very different! You mustn't park here = it is not allowed. You don't have to park here = you can park somewhere else.

📘 2. Past forms

must has no past form. Use had to: Yesterday I had to work late. For advice about the past use should have + past participle: You should have studied more. (You didn't, and it was a mistake.)

📘 3. Possibility and certainty (deduction)

How sure?VerbExample
almost sure it's truemust beHe works 12 hours a day. He must be tired.
maybemight / may / couldShe might get the job. I could be late.
almost sure it's not truecan't beThat can't be his car. He doesn't have one.

🧩 Unit 5 · Grammar: Comparing and describing: comparatives, superlatives, as ... as

🎯 Goal

You will learn to compare people, places and things, and describe them in detail.

📘 1. Comparatives (two things)

Type of adjectiveRuleExample
short (1 syllable)adjective + -er + thanRiga is bigger than Jūrmala.
ends in -y-y → -ierMy brother is funnier than me.
long (2+ syllables)more + adjective + thanTrains are more comfortable than buses.
irregulargood → better · bad → worse · far → furtherThis café is better than that one.

📘 2. Superlatives (three or more things)

TypeRuleExample
shortthe + adjective + -estIt's the oldest building in the city.
ends in -ythe + -iestShe is the happiest person I know.
longthe most + adjectiveIt's the most beautiful park in Europe.
irregularthe best · the worst · the furthestThat's the best pizza ever!

After a superlative we often use in + place or of + group: the tallest building in Latvia, the best student of all. With the present perfect: the most interesting book I have ever read.

📘 3. (not) as ... as

as + adjective + as = equal: Anna is as tall as Mara.
not as + adjective + as = less: Liepāja is not as big as Riga. (= Riga is bigger.)

📘 4. Other ways to compare

  • a bit / slightly / a little + comparative (small difference): a bit colder
  • much / far / a lot + comparative (big difference): much more expensive
  • the same as / similar to / different from: My house is different from yours.
  • the + comparative, the + comparative: The more you practise, the better you get.

📝 Unit 5 · Writing: informal and formal emails

🎯 Goal

You will learn to write informal and formal emails that describe and compare people and places, using comparatives, superlatives and linking words.

📘 1. Formal or informal?

We choose our words for the reader. We write informal emails to friends and family. We write formal emails to a boss, a teacher, a company or someone we do not know.

Informal (friends)Formal (work, school, companies)
Hi Anna, / Dear Anna,Dear Mr Brown, / Dear Ms Smith, / Dear Sir or Madam,
Thanks for your email. / Great to hear from you!Thank you for your email. / I am writing to ask about ...
Can you ...? / Could you ...?Could you please ...? / I would be grateful if you could ...
I'm sorry, but I can't ...Unfortunately, I am unable to ...
Write soon! / See you! / Take care,I look forward to hearing from you. / Thank you for your help.
Love, / Best wishes, / Bye for now,Yours sincerely, (name known) / Yours faithfully, (name not known)

Tips: In informal emails you can use short forms (I'm, can't), phrasal verbs and exclamation marks. In formal emails use full forms (I am, cannot), polite words (please, would, could) and no slang.

📘 2. A good email has four parts

  1. Greeting – Dear ... / Hi ...
  2. Reason – why you are writing (1 sentence)
  3. Main part – the details, one idea in each paragraph
  4. Ending – a closing sentence and a sign-off

📘 3. Coherence and cohesion

Coherence means your ideas are in a clear order and the reader can follow them. Use paragraphs. Put one idea in each paragraph.

Cohesion means the sentences are joined with small words. Use linking words:

UseLinking words
addingand, also, too, as well as, in addition, moreover (formal)
contrastbut, however, although, on the other hand, in spite of
reason / resultbecause, so, as, therefore, that is why
orderfirst, then, after that, finally, at the end
examplefor example, for instance, such as

Also use reference words so you do not repeat nouns: My brother has a new job. He likes it very much. This is good news.

📘 4. Unit 5 examples

✉️ Informal email

Task: Your friend is coming to visit your town. Write and describe it, and compare it with the city where your friend lives.

Hi Oleg,

I'm so happy you're coming to visit! My town is much smaller than your city, but it's also quieter and cleaner. The old town is the most beautiful part, and it's less crowded than Riga. On the other hand, there aren't as many shops, so we'll have to take the bus to the mall.

The best time to visit is in July – it's the warmest month, so we can swim in the lake. Besides, there's a music festival on 14 July. It's the biggest event of the summer!

Let me know when you're arriving.
See you soon!
Madara

✉️ Formal email

Task: You want to book a room in a hotel. Write to the hotel and ask for a quiet room in the best location.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to enquire about booking a double room from 12 to 15 August. I would prefer a room which is as quiet as possible, ideally with a view of the park rather than the street.

Furthermore, I would be grateful if you could tell me which is the cheapest room with a bathroom. Is it also possible to arrange a taxi from the airport?

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Madara Kalnina

💡 Notice

Notice the comparatives (smaller than, less crowded than, as quiet as possible) and superlatives (the most beautiful, the biggest, the cheapest). Linking words for contrast and addition: on the other hand, besides, furthermore.

🧩 Unit 6 · Grammar: Conditionals: zero, first and second

🎯 Goal

You will learn to talk about facts, real possibilities and imaginary situations, and give advice.

📘 1. Three conditionals

TypeFormUse it forExample
Zeroif + present simple, present simplefacts and things that are always trueIf you heat ice, it melts.
Firstif + present simple, will + verbreal or likely situations in the futureIf you eat well, you will feel better.
Secondif + past simple, would + verbunreal or unlikely situations; adviceIf I had more time, I would cook every day.

📘 2. Things to remember

  • The if part can come first or second. With a comma if first: If it rains, we'll stay home. Without a comma if second: We'll stay home if it rains.
  • In the first conditional, we do not use will after if: If it will rain ✗ → If it rains ✓.
  • In the second conditional, we use were for all persons: If I were you, I would see a doctor.
  • If I were you, I would ... is the most common way to give advice.
  • Instead of will you can use can, may, might, should: If you feel ill, you should rest.
  • unless = if not: You will get ill unless you sleep more.
  • as long as / provided that = only if: You can go out as long as you wear a coat.

💡 Quick test

Is it possible (maybe real)? → first conditional. Is it imaginary or unlikely? → second conditional. Is it always true? → zero conditional.

🧩 Unit 7 · Grammar: Reported speech and question tags

🎯 Goal

You will learn to report what people said and check information with question tags.

📘 1. Reported speech

We use reported speech to tell someone what another person said. Usually the verb goes one step back in time ("backshift").

Direct speechReported speech
"I work in a bank."She said she worked in a bank.
"I am tired."He said he was tired.
"I have finished."She said she had finished.
"I went home."He said he had gone home.
"I will call you."She said she would call me.
"I can swim."He said he could swim.

📘 2. Other changes

  • Pronouns change: "I like my job." → She said she liked her job.
  • Time words change: today → that day · tomorrow → the next day · yesterday → the day before · now → then · next week → the following week · ago → before
  • say + no person: She said that ... · tell + person: She told me that ...

📘 3. Reporting questions and orders

  • Questions: no question word order, no do/does/did. "Where do you live?" → He asked me where I lived.
  • Yes/no questions: use if / whether. "Are you tired?" → She asked if I was tired.
  • Orders and requests: tell / ask + person + (not) to + verb. "Open the window." → He told me to open the window.

📘 4. Question tags

A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence. We use it to check information or to ask for agreement.

SentenceTag
Positivenegative tag: You like coffee, don't you?
Negativepositive tag: She isn't here, is she?

Use the same auxiliary verb as in the sentence: It's cold, isn't it? · They have left, haven't they? · He can swim, can't he? · You went there, didn't you? Special: I am → aren't I? · Let's → shall we? · Imperative → will you?

📄 Can we trust the news?

Twenty years ago, most people got their news from television, radio or newspapers. Today, more than half of young people say that social media is their main source of news. This has changed the media world completely.

The biggest problem with online news is "fake news". A recent study found that false stories travel six times faster on social media than true ones. Some stories are written as jokes, but others are made to deceive people on purpose. "People often share a headline without reading the article," said media expert Dr Anna Vilks. "They said they didn't have time, but it took them only a minute to share it."

So how can you check if a story is true? Experts advise you to ask these questions: Who wrote the article? Does the website have a good reputation? Do other reliable sources report the same story? If the headline makes you very angry or very excited, you should be careful, because fake stories are often written to create strong emotions.

Many schools now teach "media literacy" lessons. In one Latvian school, the teacher told the students to find a false story online and explain how they knew it was false. "It was a great exercise," one student said. "I'll never share a story without checking it again."

🎯 Goal

You will learn to write informal and formal emails that report news and give opinions, using reported speech, question tags and linking words.

📘 1. Formal or informal?

📘 2. A good email has four parts

  1. Greeting – Dear ... / Hi ...
  2. Reason – why you are writing (1 sentence)
  3. Main part – the details, one idea in each paragraph
  4. Ending – a closing sentence and a sign-off

📘 3. Coherence and cohesion

Coherence means your ideas are in a clear order and the reader can follow them. Use paragraphs. Put one idea in each paragraph.

Cohesion means the sentences are joined with small words. Use linking words:

UseLinking words
addingand, also, too, as well as, in addition, moreover (formal)
contrastbut, however, although, on the other hand, in spite of
reason / resultbecause, so, as, therefore, that is why
orderfirst, then, after that, finally, at the end
examplefor example, for instance, such as

📘 4. Unit 7 examples

✉️ Informal email

Task: You heard some news about your town. Write to a friend to tell them what happened and what people said.

Hi Janis,

Have you heard the news? The council announced that they were going to build a new park next to the river! The mayor said it would be finished by next summer. You'll love it, won't you? It's close to your flat.

Not everybody is happy, though. My neighbour told me that the park would bring too much noise. However, I think it's a great idea, because it will make our town greener. Besides, they said they would plant two hundred trees.

Do you want to come to the opening? Let me know!
Take care,
Kristine

✉️ Formal email

Task: You read an article in a newspaper and you disagree. Write a letter to the editor with your opinion.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing in response to your article, "Free transport for all", which was published on 5 May. The article said that free public transport would reduce pollution. However, I do not believe that this is the case.

Firstly, the minister claimed that thousands of people would stop using their cars, but there was no evidence for this. Secondly, the money to pay for the buses will have to come from taxes. Therefore, I would suggest spending the money on better cycle paths instead.

I hope you will consider publishing my opinion.

Yours faithfully,
Kristine Bērziņa

💡 Notice

Both emails use reported speech (the mayor said it would be finished, the article said that...). The informal email uses a question tag (You'll love it, won't you?). In the formal letter note: I am writing in response to ..., Firstly, Secondly, Therefore, I would suggest.

AreaFormExample

📝 Unit 8 · Writing: informal and formal emails

🎯 Goal

You will learn to write informal and formal emails about shopping and money, using all the B1 grammar you have studied and linking words.

📘 1. Formal or informal?

We choose our words for the reader. We write informal emails to friends and family. We write formal emails to a boss, a teacher, a company or someone we do not know.

Informal (friends)Formal (work, school, companies)
Hi Anna, / Dear Anna,Dear Mr Brown, / Dear Ms Smith, / Dear Sir or Madam,
Thanks for your email. / Great to hear from you!Thank you for your email. / I am writing to ask about ...
Can you ...? / Could you ...?Could you please ...? / I would be grateful if you could ...
I'm sorry, but I can't ...Unfortunately, I am unable to ...
Write soon! / See you! / Take care,I look forward to hearing from you. / Thank you for your help.
Love, / Best wishes, / Bye for now,Yours sincerely, (name known) / Yours faithfully, (name not known)

Tips: In informal emails you can use short forms (I'm, can't), phrasal verbs and exclamation marks. In formal emails use full forms (I am, cannot), polite words (please, would, could) and no slang.

📘 2. A good email has four parts

  1. Greeting – Dear ... / Hi ...
  2. Reason – why you are writing (1 sentence)
  3. Main part – the details, one idea in each paragraph
  4. Ending – a closing sentence and a sign-off

📘 3. Coherence and cohesion

Coherence means your ideas are in a clear order and the reader can follow them. Use paragraphs. Put one idea in each paragraph.

Cohesion means the sentences are joined with small words. Use linking words:

UseLinking words
addingand, also, too, as well as, in addition, moreover (formal)
contrastbut, however, although, on the other hand, in spite of
reason / resultbecause, so, as, therefore, that is why
orderfirst, then, after that, finally, at the end
examplefor example, for instance, such as

Also use reference words so you do not repeat nouns: My brother has a new job. He likes it very much. This is good news.

📘 4. Unit 8 examples

✉️ Informal email

Task: Your friend borrowed money and wants to know when you need it back. Also tell them about something you bought last week.

Hi Karlis,

Thanks for your message! Don't worry about the money – you can give it back next month. I know you're saving for a new bike, aren't you?

By the way, I bought some new trainers last week. They were on sale, so they only cost 40 euros instead of 80. What a bargain! However, they were a bit too big, so I had to exchange them. Next time I will try them on first!

Let me know if you want to meet at the weekend. If it doesn't rain, we could go for a walk.

Best wishes,
Mara

✉️ Formal email

Task: You bought a product online but it arrived damaged. Write to the company to complain and ask for a refund.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about a coffee machine which I ordered from your website on 12 May (order number 7421). When the parcel arrived, I noticed that the machine was broken. Unfortunately, it cannot be used.

I paid 120 euros for it, so I would be grateful if you could send me a full refund. I have attached my receipt and photographs of the damage. If I do not receive a reply within ten days, I will contact the consumer protection office.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Mara Ozola

💡 Notice

These emails use many tenses: past simple (bought, cost), present perfect, first conditional (If it doesn't rain, ...), quantity words (too big, enough), a question tag (aren't you?) and the passive (cannot be used). Linking words: however, by the way, so, unfortunately, if.

Write to a friend. Tell them about something you bought recently, say whether you are happy with it, and suggest meeting.

✉️ Option B: formal
